introduction-its-not-magic-its-linux.core: A container is an ordinary Linux process with restricted views and limits: namespaces isolate what it sees (PIDs, network, mounts, users, hostname, IPC), cgroups limit what it can use (CPU, memory, I/O), and a layered root filesystem provides its files. There's no hypervisor; containers share the host kernel.

first_principles.problem: Engineers treat containers as lightweight VMs and are surprised by shared-kernel behaviour and security limits.
truths: Processes can be given private views of the system.
Resource usage can be capped per group of processes.
A filesystem can be assembled from layers.
derivation: Shared **kernel** → lighter but weaker isolation than VMs.

analogy.title: An office worker in a cubicle with blinkers and a budget
analogy.story: They only see their own desk, can spend only their allowance, but share the building's power and plumbing.
analogy.breaks: Cubicle walls are physical; namespace isolation can be escaped through kernel bugs.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The 'container' is a process with namespaces and cgroups.

code.text:
docker run -d --name web nginx
ps -ef | grep nginx            # just a host process
lsns -p $(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' web)
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/docker-*.scope/memory.max

check.q: What do cgroups provide for containers?
check.a: Resource limits and accounting for CPU, memory, I/O and other resources.

image-layers-the-union-filesystem.core: An image is a stack of read-only layers, each the filesystem diff from one build step, identified by content hash. OverlayFS merges them into one view and adds a thin writable layer per container (copy-on-write). Layers are shared and cached across images, so ordering Dockerfile steps from least to most frequently changing speeds builds.

first_principles.problem: Every code change triggers a full dependency reinstall and a 1 GB image push.
truths: Unchanged layers are cached by hash.
A changed layer invalidates all layers after it.
derivation: Put **rarely changing steps first** (base, OS packages, dependencies).
**Combine** related RUN commands and clean up in the same layer.

analogy.title: Transparent sheets stacked on an overhead projector
analogy.story: Each sheet adds or covers something; you see the combined picture, and only the top sheet is writable.
analogy.breaks: Erasing on a lower sheet is impossible; deleting a file in a later layer only hides it, it still takes space.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Code edits rebuild only the last layer.

code.text:
FROM node:22-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

check.q: Why copy package.json before the source code?
check.a: So the dependency install layer stays cached when only source files change.

multi-stage-builds-the-builder-pattern.core: Multi-stage builds use several FROM stages in one Dockerfile: a fat build stage with compilers and dev dependencies produces artefacts, and a slim final stage copies only those artefacts (COPY --from=build). The shipped image contains no toolchain, which makes it smaller, faster to pull and with less attack surface.

first_principles.problem: A Go service image is 1.2 GB because it includes the whole Go toolchain and source.
truths: Build tools aren't needed at runtime.

analogy.title: A factory and a showroom
analogy.story: Products are made in the messy factory; only the finished goods go to the showroom.
analogy.breaks: Showrooms display everything nicely; final images still need any runtime libraries the artefact depends on.

code.text:
FROM golang:1.23 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /out/api ./cmd/api

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12
COPY --from=build /out/api /api
USER nonroot
ENTRYPOINT ["/api"]

check.a: Copies files from an earlier build stage into the current stage.

distroless-images-the-ultimate-minimalis.core: Distroless images contain only your app and its runtime dependencies (libc, CA certificates, timezone data, language runtime), with no shell, package manager or utilities. That shrinks size and CVE counts and removes tools attackers use, but debugging requires ephemeral debug containers or :debug variants.

first_principles.problem: Security scans flag hundreds of CVEs in packages the app never uses (bash, curl, apt).
truths: Apps need only a few runtime files.
derivation: Pick the right variant (**static, base, cc, java, python**).

analogy.title: A sealed appliance with no user-serviceable parts
analogy.story: It does one job, and there are no tools inside for tampering.
analogy.breaks: Appliances can be opened by technicians; distroless needs a separate debug image to inspect.

example.title: CVE comparison
flow: No shell for attackers to exec into

check.q: Why must distroless images use exec-form ENTRYPOINT?
check.a: There's no shell to interpret shell-form commands.

buildkit-the-modern-docker-builder.core: BuildKit is Docker's modern build engine: it builds stages in parallel, skips unused stages, supports cache mounts (persist package caches between builds), secret mounts (use credentials without baking them into layers), SSH forwarding, multi-platform builds via buildx and remote/registry cache export for CI.

first_principles.problem: CI builds take 15 minutes because dependency caches are lost each run, and a token ended up in an image layer.
truths: Independent stages can run in parallel.
Package caches can be reused safely.

analogy.title: A modern kitchen with several cooks and a shared pantry
analogy.story: Dishes are prepped in parallel, staples are kept between services, and the safe key is never left on the counter.
analogy.breaks: Kitchens reuse leftovers freely; cache mounts aren't included in the final image.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Faster installs; token never stored in a layer.

code.text:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM python:3.12-slim
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip \
    --mount=type=secret,id=pip_token \
    PIP_INDEX_URL=https://$(cat /run/secrets/pip_token)@pypi.example.com/simple \
    pip install -r requirements.txt

check.q: How do you use a credential during a build without leaving it in the image?

entrypoint-vs-cmd-the-eternal-confusion.core: ENTRYPOINT defines the executable that always runs; CMD supplies default arguments (or a default command if there's no ENTRYPOINT). docker run args replace CMD, and --entrypoint overrides ENTRYPOINT. Use exec form (JSON arrays) so the process runs as PID 1 and receives signals; shell form wraps it in /bin/sh -c.

first_principles.problem: docker run myimage --debug fails because the flag replaced the whole command instead of being appended.
truths: Shell form inserts a shell process.
derivation: Use an **entrypoint script** with exec "$@" for setup.

analogy.title: A coffee machine and its default order
analogy.story: The machine (ENTRYPOINT) always makes coffee; the default is a latte (CMD) unless you ask for something else.
analogy.breaks: Coffee machines don't care about signals; shell-form entrypoints can swallow SIGTERM.

code.text:
ENTRYPOINT ["/app/server"]
CMD ["--port=8080"]
# docker run img            → /app/server --port=8080
# docker run img --debug    → /app/server --debug

check.q: In Kubernetes, which field overrides a Docker ENTRYPOINT?
check.a: The container's command field (args overrides CMD).

signals-handling-and-the-pid-1-problem.core: The first process in a container is PID 1. Linux gives PID 1 special behaviour: it doesn't get default signal handlers (SIGTERM is ignored unless handled) and must reap zombie child processes. Shell-form entrypoints or apps without handlers cause slow, forced shutdowns (SIGKILL after the grace period) and zombie build-up. Use exec form, handle SIGTERM, or add a tiny init (tini, --init).

first_principles.problem: Pods take the full 30-second grace period to stop and then get killed, dropping in-flight requests.
derivation: Use **tini / docker run --init / shareProcessNamespace** to reap zombies.

analogy.title: A shop manager who must lock up and send staff home
analogy.story: If the manager ignores the closing bell, security eventually throws everyone out mid-sale.
analogy.breaks: Managers notice bells; a process only reacts to signals it registers handlers for.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Clean stop in seconds, no dropped requests.

code.text:
import signal, sys
def shutdown(signum, frame):
    server.stop_accepting(); server.drain(timeout=20); sys.exit(0)
signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, shutdown)

check.q: Why does a shell-form ENTRYPOINT break graceful shutdown?
check.a: The shell becomes PID 1 and doesn't forward SIGTERM to the app, so it's eventually SIGKILLed.
